name: Mind Mapping
use_case: I have to write a report, a proposal or a plan on a topic I know plenty about, but my thoughts on it are a jumble: I don't know where to start, which pieces belong together or what I have left out, and I want to see the shape of the whole before I write the first sentence.
strengths: fast to start: one word in the middle of a blank page, no template, no software and no training needed
gets everything a person knows onto one page, so gaps and lopsided parts of a topic become visible at a glance
the main branches turn directly into the chapters of a text, the sections of a plan or the parts of a talk
keywords instead of sentences keep the writer from polishing wording before the structure is clear
works for one person at a desk and equally as a shared drawing on a whiteboard or in a simple online tool
easy to extend later: a forgotten point is added to its branch without rewriting anything
weaknesses: every point must sit under exactly one branch, so topics whose parts influence each other are forced into a tree that hides the links between them
it orders a topic but does not weigh, rank or decide anything; choosing between options needs a separate step
a map is often readable only by its author, because the keywords and private abbreviations carry meaning nobody else shares
large maps become cluttered and hard to read, and their hierarchy usually needs redrawing more than once
it captures what the author already knows; it does not by itself produce new information or test whether that knowledge is right
research support is modest: controlled studies on mind maps are few and small, and strong claims in popular books about memory and brain power go well beyond the evidence
use_cases: I have to write a concept for the new library at our school and so far it is all a muddle in my mind; I cannot see where to begin or how the various parts fit together.

A project officer in a municipal office has to draft the plan for a new neighbourhood service; what she knows is spread across meeting notes, e-mails and her own thoughts, and she wants to gather all of it on one page and group it before she writes an outline.

Pupils who are asked to write an essay or prepare a presentation keep getting stuck on the first sentence; the teacher wants them to set down everything they know about the subject first, grouped into a few main points, and only then decide on an order.
A student working through a long lecture or a dense report wants notes on a single page that show how the points relate to the main subject, instead of pages of sentences copied down line by line.
audience: anyone preparing a text, plan or talk
